items.title: A weird experiment I've been trying the last few weeks is having Claude take over day-to-day mainten...
items.content:
A weird experiment I've been trying the last few weeks is having Claude take over day-to-day maintenance of our apps. Seeing early signs of life that this might be possible.

The setup is straightforward: we have a Slack channel called proj-claude-maintains-apps. In it, Claude Tag runs a bunch of daily routines across iOS, Android, Desktop, web, CLI, and Agent SDK:

- Crash fuzzer: open the app in a simulator and tap around to find ways to crash it, then root cause and fix the crashes
- Dup unifier: scans the codebase for similar-yet-slightly-divergent abstractions, and puts up PRs to unify them
- Dead-code remover: removes statically unreachable code, and adds logging to suspected dead code to check if it's really dead and if so, remove it the next day
- Abstraction police: fixes leaky abstractions
- a bunch more..

Results have been surprisingly positive. Over the last few weeks, these routines have opened 388 PRs across our repos, 180 of which we merged after Claude Code Review + human review. We're now thinking about how to streamline this to make merging these kinds of mechanical changes easier.

Claude generally gets these PRs right on the first shot, and if it doesn't, we ask Claude to tune its routines so it's better the next day. Sometimes it takes a few days of tuning. 

To try a similar workflow, ask Claude Code or Tag, or create some routines directly at https://t.co/Z70hStEBH6. A few of the actual prompts I used below.

Has anyone experimented with similar workflows?

items.title: Google has released Gemini 3.7 Flash, improving 4 points over Gemini 3.6 Flash and reaching the Inte...
items.content:
Google has released Gemini 3.7 Flash, improving 4 points over Gemini 3.6 Flash and reaching the Intelligence vs. Time per Task Pareto frontier

@GoogleDeepMind has released its third new Gemini Flash model in three months. Gemini 3.7 Flash (high) scores 56 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, just behind GPT-5.6 Terra (max, 57) and Muse Spark 1.2 (xhigh, 57)

We benchmarked Gemini 3.7 Flash across all three reasoning levels (high, medium, low) ahead of release. With high reasoning, Gemini 3.7 Flash is a 4 point improvement over 3.6 Flash, while achieving an average Time per Task of 1.7, 40% faster than GPT-5.6 Terra (max). This places Gemini 3.7 Flash on the Intelligence vs. Time per Task Pareto frontier, reinforcing Google’s focus on speed across the Gemini Flash family of models

Key benchmarking results across Gemini 3.7 Flash’s three reasoning levels:

➤ 4 point Intelligence Index improvement: Gemini 3.7 Flash (high) scores 56 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, up 4 points from Gemini 3.6 Flash. The improvement is driven primarily by gains on agentic evaluations, including Tau3 Banking (+3 points), Terminal-Bench v2.1 (+8 points), and GDPval-AA v2 (+103 Elo). With medium reasoning, Gemini 3.7 Flash scores 53, matching DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 (max, 53) and GLM-5.2 (max, 53). With low reasoning, it scores 51, just behind DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 (max, 52)

➤ Pareto frontier on Intelligence vs. Time per Task: Gemini 3.7 Flash produces ~340 output tokens per second, nearly 3x the output speed of GPT-5.6 Terra and GLM-5.2. With high reasoning, this translates to an average Time per Task of 1.7 minutes, placing Gemini 3.7 Flash on the Intelligence vs. Time per Task Pareto frontier

➤ 30% lower Cost per Task than Gemini 3.6 Flash: Gemini 3.7 Flash retains Gemini 3.6 Flash’s standard pricing of $1.50/$7.50 per 1M input/output tokens, however Google is offering discounted pricing through the end of the year at $0.75/$3.75 per 1M tokens. At this discounted price, Gemini 3.7 Flash (high) costs $0.40 per Intelligence Index task, 30% less than Gemini 3.6 Flash and matching Muse Spark 1.2 (xhigh, $0.40). With medium reasoning, Cost per Task falls to $0.26, placing the model on the Intelligence vs. Cost per Task Pareto frontier

➤ Leading performance on AutomationBench-AA and AA-AnalystAgent: On AA-AnalystAgent, our recently released benchmark measuring models’ ability to answer complex questions about spreadsheets and documents, Gemini 3.7 Flash (high) achieves the highest pass^5 score at 60%, ahead of Claude Opus 5 (max, 54%) and Fable 5 (49%). Gemini 3.7 Flash also leads AutomationBench-AA, our benchmark of agentic capabilities in simulated SaaS environments, with a score of 62.7%, ahead of Kimi K3 (max, 53%) and GPT-5.6 Sol (max, 51.2%)

Key model details:

➤ Context Window: 1M tokens, unchanged from Gemini 3.6 Flash

➤ Multimodality: Text, image, video, and speech input, with text output

➤ Pricing: $1.50/$7.50 per 1M input/output tokens at standard pricing. Google is offering discounted pricing of $0.75/$3.75 per 1M tokens through the end of the year. Cached input tokens retain the same 90% discount

items.title:
A crucial ingredient missing from most AI models: the ability to understand the physical world.

The...
items.content:
A crucial ingredient missing from most AI models: the ability to understand the physical world.

The best way to gain that understanding is to learn the continuous functions, the underlying mathematical relationships, that fully describe those systems.

But many AI models were created for language processing or computer vision, where data can be treated as collections of isolated points, such as words in a sentence or a fixed set of pixels in an image.

Instead, we propose a Neural Operator framework that shows how to extend existing neural network architectures in a way that allows AI systems to learn continuous functions.

We take popular architectures like convolutional neural nets, transforms, graph neural nets and extend them to Neural Operators in a principled way.

Thank you @Caltech  for covering our work appearing in @Nature https://t.co/DRogL2prLH @mliuschi @JeanKossaifi @julberner

items.title: The way most people leverage test-time compute today is via a form of test-time NL reasoning that is...
items.content:
The way most people leverage test-time compute today is via a form of test-time NL reasoning that is computationally equivalent to test-time search (sometimes with a verifier / grader in the loop). The other major avenue to leverage test-time compute is test-time training. Gradients are a precious signal, there's no reason not to use it at test time (other than the fact that it would be difficult / expensive from an engineering standpoint).

https://t.co/BYpnjtO9Nf

items.reasoning: Original technical framing on inference-time scaling from a leading researcher; useful taxonomy for a live research debate despite modest likes.

items.title: We’re launching Optima. Now anyone can create a custom benchmark for their use case, leveraging Arti...
items.content:
We’re launching Optima. Now anyone can create a custom benchmark for their use case, leveraging Artificial Analysis’ leading research and platform

Building and running benchmarks is difficult. We have distilled Artificial Analysis’ research and experience developing benchmarks into Optima, a new platform for benchmarking models on your own workloads and comparing performance, speed and cost efficiency. Optima allows you to find the best model for your task, or an equally performant alternative to your current setup at 10x lower cost or time per task.

We’ve integrated Artificial Analysis' research and experience in benchmarks across the Optima workflow:

➤ Build benchmarks based on your own data and use cases: There are three ways to build a benchmark with Optima. Upload an existing evaluation dataset from your own files or @huggingface, or import agent traces from platforms including @arizeai, @braintrust and @langfuse. Install the Optima skill to build a benchmark using context from your coding environment and previous sessions. Or simply describe your use case and provide example inputs and outputs, and Optima will build the benchmark for you

➤ Run across the latest models: Run the same benchmark across leading models in a single click, and keep your leaderboard up to date as soon as new models are released

➤ Bring Artificial Analysis grading to your own benchmark: Evaluate responses against objective rubric criteria or using the same pairwise judging approach used for Artificial Analysis benchmarks including GDPval-AA and AA-Briefcase. For pairwise judging, select your preferred responses from a sample and Optima uses those preferences to rank models across your test set

➤ Compare performance, cost and time efficiency: Optima measures more than model performance. Cost per Task and Time per Task are tracked alongside benchmark scores, with category-level results and support for custom metrics, allowing you to compare the tradeoffs between models for your specific use case

Ahead of launch, here are examples questions our beta testers answered with Optima:

➤ Which model can save me 10x the cost without a meaningful decrease in quality for my finance & accounting agent?

➤ Which model best matches the writing style of lawyers for my legal agent?

➤ Which model can best identify different elements in my custom image dataset?

Optima is available today. Build your own benchmark at https://t.co/LKMSqnhA0D

items.title: Matrix-based optimizers such as Muon, which use the structure of an entire weight matrix when choosi...
items.content:
Matrix-based optimizers such as Muon, which use the structure of an entire weight matrix when choosing an update, can train language models faster than AdamW, but earlier gains tended to shrink as models and training runs became larger, suggesting that part of the problem might lie not in the optimizer itself but in how weight decay controls the size of the weights during training. 

In this paper, the authors from @Princeton, @Stanford, and @Tsinghua_Uni introduce Hyperball, a wrapper that fixes both the size of each weight matrix and the size of its optimizer update, where “size” means the ordinary Euclidean length of all the matrix entries taken together; this makes the learning rate directly control how far the matrix changes in direction instead of letting that behavior emerge indirectly through weight decay.

On Qwen3-style models up to 1.2 billion parameters, Muon with Hyperball needs about 20–30% fewer tokens than an AdamW baseline to reach the same loss, and its best learning rate changes much less when model depth or width changes.

Read with an AI tutor: https://t.co/tXD9r5gM3x

items.title: This week we launched the world's most accurate document extraction agent over real-world documents....
items.content:
This week we launched the world's most accurate document extraction agent over real-world documents.

Introducing LlamaExtract Agentic Plus 💫 . It is a complete document extraction model+harness engine that can convert even the most complex document types/lengths/schemas into clean, grounded, structured output.

We benchmarked it over ExtractBench - a comprehensive set of real-world enterprise documents. It is measured over various dimensions: document length (short/medium/long), task (long-list, needle in haystack, dense docs), perception (rotated, scanned, handwriting), table structured (merged headers, cross-page tables, table within cells), and business domains.

We compared it against a variety of coding agent harness to document extraction solutions. LlamaExtract Agentic Plus is not only highly accurate, it is quite price efficient relative to its capabilities (25-50% the price of Claude Code/Codex).

You can see the full release of ExtractBench here: https://t.co/tsXfovKJaz

If you want to check it out, come sign up for an account on LlamaParse: https://t.co/XYZmx5T7JA

items.content:
New session w/@sh_reya where she goes over a useful new eval called the Data Agent Benchmark (DAB).  

Data agents answer business questions like “which cohort had the highest churn?” that a data analyst would normally answer.  

DAB recreates the mess of a real data warehouse. Each task spreads data across at least two database systems, with inconsistent join keys, key values buried in free text, and ambiguous or ill-defined schemas.

Google DeepMind just shipped a model that lets people sign into a Pixel 11 instead of typing.

SL2T starts with ASL-to-English in Gboard and Live Transcribe.

Testers said signing was faster than typing in English.

To keep the camera feed private, the phone tracks points on the hands, face, and body on-device and discards the video.

Sam Sepah, a Deaf Googler, originated the project.

Demis Hassabis: “Built in close collaboration with the Deaf community, it’s a great example of the good that can be done with AI.”

What I can tell you is what's working for the people I work with and me.

We aren't manually reading the code anymore. We don't care about individual lines. We don't have anybody trying to understand the thousands of AI-generated lines we get.

Instead, we have designed (and continue to invest here) automated processes to verify that we are shipping high-quality software,

The quality of our software hasn’t gone down in any way, shape, or form. We are delivering more and faster.

People are working the same amount of time, but the nature of their work has changed significantly.

I don't know what you are building and how you are doing it, so I'm not going to pretend I can speak about how you should do it.

If you find value in reading AI-generated code, good for you! If you think that's the best way for you to verify the software you build is good, then keep doing it.

items.title:
85% say the bottleneck is reviewing AI code, not writing it.

@gitlab asked 1,528 developers and buy...
items.content:
85% say the bottleneck is reviewing AI code, not writing it.

@gitlab asked 1,528 developers and buyers. The queue moved from generation to validation.

@SonarSource's 1,100+ survey says 42% of committed code is AI-generated. 96% do not fully trust it is functionally correct. Only 48% always check before they commit.

We generate faster than anyone can read. Another round of doubt will not shrink that queue.

@unclebobmartin ships unread agent code. He can, because the checks fail it without him:

> Unit tests he never reads
> Acceptance tests he spot-checks
> Mutation on the suite
> Quality metrics on the output

The transferable part is not his full stack. It is how much autonomy a change earns when something cheap can fail it. Reading every line just makes you the new queue.

> When can a change ship unread?
> What still needs a name on it if it ships wrong?
> What fails if nobody reads the diff?

Full Breakdown ↓↓

items.title: A positive Claude watermark doesn’t prove it’s entirely AI-generated and the lack of a watermark doe...
items.content:
A positive Claude watermark doesn’t prove it’s entirely AI-generated and the lack of a watermark doesn’t prove it’s entirely human-generated. 

The two best ways to tell if something is AI-generated:

1) Use AI so much that you notice the telltale signs (“quiet”, “here’s the truth:”)

2) Compare against hundreds of others responses to the same question (ex: when we have a job application out, we can tell that half of the responses are nearly identical in structure and content) 

And unlike Pokémon, you’ll never catch ‘em all. And yes I wrote that myself.

items.summary: Argument that AI provenance watermarks are neither necessary nor sufficient evidence of machine authorship, and that the practical detection methods are heavy personal familiarity with model idioms and comparing many responses to the same prompt for structural sameness.

items.title: We put $2,500 on the first person who could get a pizza delivered to the room by an AI agent they ha...
items.content:
We put $2,500 on the first person who could get a pizza delivered to the room by an AI agent they hadn't written yet.

They had 90 minutes to write it, with the clock running on the projector and no pre built code allowed.

That was AlphaSignal's Pizza Agent Challenge in SF last week.

750 people registered and around 130 turned up to build. Engineers from OpenAI, Google, AWS, Palantir, Goldman Sachs and JP Morgan signed up for it.

The mission was to build an agent that autonomously orders a pepperoni jalapeño pizza and gets it delivered to the venue. First box through the door wins.

Checkout is where most of them got stuck, because the agent had to place a real order with real money against a real merchant.

The winner took first by building on the DoorDash CLI that shipped last month. Second and third pushed their orders through @Brave's API, which held up. 

Thanks to @Naamoney_ for running it with us, and to @Brave for backing it. 

If you had 90 minutes and no pre written code, how would you have gotten the order through?
items.author: @AlphaSignalAI
items.summary: Newsletter account recaps a live agent-building contest in San Francisco where participants had 90 minutes and no pre-written code to build an agent that autonomously orders and pays for a pizza delivery, with checkout and real payments as the main failure point.
items.reasoning: Useful concrete signal about the state of agentic commerce, where payment and checkout remain the hard part, and about which merchant CLIs and APIs actually work; self-promotional framing and very low engagement limit it.

We put $2,500 on the first person who could get a pizza delivered to the room by an AI agent they hadn't written yet.

The mission was to build an agent that autonomously orders a pepperoni jalapeño pizza and gets it delivered to the venue. First box through the door wins.

Checkout is where most of them got stuck, because the agent had to place a real order with real money against a real merchant.

items.title: Shadow AI is what happens when employees use unapproved AI tools to work faster, often without the c...
items.content:
Shadow AI is what happens when employees use unapproved AI tools to work faster, often without the company knowing how data is used or exposed.

It may look like a personal shortcut, but the risk does not stay personal.

Microblog  by  @antgrasso  about  #AIGovernance #ShadowAI 

An employee pastes a customer email into a public AI tool to draft a faster reply.

The task is completed in minutes, yet sensitive information may now sit outside company safeguards.

The same pattern can spread quietly. Teams begin depending on tools that security cannot assess and the organization cannot support.

A useful shortcut has started shaping the way work gets done.

Simply telling people to stop is unlikely to solve the problem. 

Organizations need approved alternatives that are easy to use, along with clear guidance on which information can enter an AI system. 

Employees should also have a simple way to ask questions before choosing a tool on their own.

Shadow AI usually points to a gap between how people need to work and what the company currently provides.

You cannot govern AI use that employees feel they must hide.
items.author: @antgrasso
items.summary: Essay on shadow AI, describing how employees pasting sensitive data into unapproved tools creates governance gaps, and arguing organizations need approved alternatives and clear data-entry guidance rather than bans.
items.reasoning: Substantive enterprise governance argument with strong share rate for its audience; practical rather than novel, and from a commentator rather than a researcher.

🪲 Known Bugs: August 2026

Hey everyone!

We've seen a jump in bug reports this past week and want you to know the team is actively working on resolving them.

Issues we're tracking right now:

-Edit / delete / rewind / pin menu (long-press) opens slowly and won't respond to taps

-Messages going blank or disappearing when scrolling

-Persona list won't scroll or the selected persona doesn't stick

-App freezing or not responding to taps

Most of these are affecting the app specifically if you're stuck, please use the website for now.
Fixes are in progress and some issues are already improving. 
You can also track the progress here: https://t.co/4LEvqLB6tH

Thanks for your patience and for all the reports! Please visit our help center if you run into any other issues: https://t.co/EspGwmOmTk

So me and @theannalux our trip in December last year was:

🇨🇳 Fly into Beijing ...
items.content:
Oh dudeeee no way! 

So me and @theannalux our trip in December last year was:

🇨🇳 Fly into Beijing (we came from Japan)

Stayed in Aman Summer Palace was a cool experience (now ex Aman)

Then after 2 days flew to Chengdu, stayed there a week, very fun city, we also went to see the pandas, and try the best hotpot in the world

Then high speed train to Chongqing, quite a tourist place but cool for a few days, then high speed train back to Chengdu

Then we flew to Shanghai and an AI company guy there kindly drove us too Hangzhou to check the AI companies there, we visited Alibaba AI very interesting

If you wanna see more tourist/nature stuff Guilin is cool (big mountains)

One thing to know is Google Maps is all wrong in China, because they use some GPS encryption for military reasons, so use Amap! And install Alipay, connect your payment card, via Alipay you can use lots of apps like Didi (Uber of China), many of these apps inside Alipay won't work for foreigners outside of it (or not easy)

Also internet can be challenging, I got an eSIM from Airalo for Asia and it worked to go outside the firewall

Also if you go with family maybe helps to find some local fixer or agent, nobody speaks English (but ppl helpful), so sometimes you can have a difficult situation if you have no Chinese speaker with you. Normally I'd not book tourist tours to for ex Chinese Wall but in China I would because it means you get essentially a local fixer/translator

Food can be difficult too but if you get a good hotel you can just eat Western food there. A good China-only hotel is called Niccolo Hotels, very luxurious, clean and actually great prices too

Have fun!!!!

More testing and body scans etc will shows lots of issues that are not actually issues but might become issues the moment you start cutting in people's body

But the benefits of preventative healthcare if we do it right will still outweigh the negatives of that

Also with cheap and regular testing (like the Midjourney Medical scanner) you can see your body change and quickly spot irregularities

Being against longevity and preventative healthcare because it has its issues is kinda like being against cars in 1900 because they kill people, they do but the benefits outweighed that over staying with horses

items.title: People who don’t understand how social media works fail to grasp the *social* aspect of social media...
items.content: People who don’t understand how social media works fail to grasp the *social* aspect of social media. When *normal* people hang out with each other they don’t care how “original” topics of conversation are. They just care about having something - anything - to talk about for the sake of companionship, fellowship, or communion. I have family members who have told me the same old story for the gazzillionth time and I don’t mind a bit because I care about them as very dear persons, and not as mechanical sources of information.

@Ldnbox It depends on many things

Which water do you use? I use natural mineral water

Which coffee beans do you use? Most coffee tastes shit and is low quality, I import premium beans from Brazil

How much grounds do you use? Do you have a scale? I use 15-20g

What temperature is your water? Mine is 95C

How fast do you pour over? The first pour should just make all the grounds only wet, then stop there, then once it's fully drained continue with more water

Do you have a goose neck pour over kettle? It's hard to pour over with a regular kettle, as you'll flood the coffee with water
